findings.claim: Straw mulch on steep burned slopes lowered first-winter sediment yield in a trial.
findings.conditions: slopes steeper than 30 percent, first winter after fire
findings.excerpt: straw mulch reduced sediment yield by 50-70% during the first winter after the fire

findings.claim: Biochar at moderate volume rates increased the water holding capacity of a sandy loam in a greenhouse.
findings.excerpt: biochar applied at 5-10% by volume raised the water holding capacity

findings.claim: Growers reported less wind erosion on fields kept under winter cover.
findings.excerpt: Growers in the fixture survey reported less wind erosion on fields kept covered all winter

candidate_strategies.name: Winter cereal rye cover after harvest
candidate_strategies.summary: Establish a grass or cereal cover crop (cereal rye, oats, annual ryegrass, triticale, or sorghum-sudangrass) after harvest or between cash crops. Their fibrous, extensive root systems scavenge residual soil nitrogen, add large amounts of surface residue and organic matter, and provide strong erosion control during otherwise bare fallow periods.
actions: Choose a grass species for winter hardiness (cereal rye/triticale) or summer growth (sorghum-sudangrass)
Drill or broadcast seed promptly after cash-crop harvest
Allow fall and/or spring growth to scavenge residual nitrogen and build residue
Mow, roll-crimp, or allow winterkill (oats) to terminate before the next crop
Favor deep-rooted species such as sudangrass where compaction relief is also needed
candidate_strategies.timing: planted immediately after cash-crop harvest in late summer/fall; terminated in spring before the next crop
candidate_strategies.time_to_effect: erosion protection within weeks of establishment; organic matter benefits accrue over several seasons
benefits: adds large amounts of root and surface residue
provides very effective erosion control while adding significant quantities of organic matter
annual ryegrass roots may grow 3-4 feet deep
risks_limitations: mature grass residue has a high C:N ratio and can tie up nitrogen for the next crop
some species (annual ryegrass) can become difficult-to-control weeds if not terminated on time

sources.excerpt: Cereal rye planted right after harvest protects bare cropland soil through winter storms.
